Eclipse-phase target-cell-limited viral kinetics

Source: R/model_eclipse.R
eclipse_trajectory.Rd

The within-host model used in the SARS-CoV-2 application: $$\dot U = -\beta U V, \quad \dot I_1 = \beta U V - \kappa I_1, \quad \dot I_2 = \kappa I_1 - \delta I_2, \quad \dot V = p I_2 - cV,$$ with \(U(0) = T_0\), \(I_1(0) = I_2(0) = 0\) and \(V(0) = V_0\). The eclipse compartment \(I_1\) is what separates this from the basic target-cell-limited model: without it a newly infected cell produces virus immediately, which the observed rise is too slow to support.

Usage

eclipse_trajectory(
  times,
  beta,
  delta,
  p,
  V0,
  kappa = 4,
  c_clear = 10,
  T0 = 1e+07,
  grid = seq(0, max(times) + 1, by = 0.1)
)

Arguments

times

Numeric vector of times (days) at which to return viral load.

beta, delta, p, V0

Free parameters: infection rate constant, infected-cell loss rate, virion production rate, inoculum.

kappa, c_clear, T0

Fixed constants. Defaults are the values adopted by Ke et al. (2021) for the upper respiratory tract. T0 is a scale convention rather than a literature value: it enters only through the products \(\beta T_0\) and \(p T_0\), so rescaling it and compensating in beta and p leaves the trajectory unchanged.

grid

Internal solver grid.

Value

A numeric vector of viral load at times.

References

Baccam P et al. (2006) Kinetics of influenza A virus infection in humans. J Virol 80, 7590-7599.

Ke R et al. (2021) In vivo kinetics of SARS-CoV-2 infection and its relationship with a person's infectiousness. PNAS 118, e2111477118.

See also

eclipse_design()

Examples

if (requireNamespace("deSolve", quietly = TRUE)) {
  v <- eclipse_trajectory(0:20, beta = 3e-8, delta = 1.7, p = 45, V0 = 10)
  round(log10(v[c(1, 6, 11)]), 2)
}
#> [1]  1.00 -0.52 -1.02
